Q: Is there any way we can help Stack Overflow Website get back up? A:

There already exist various versions of StackOverflow in different languages. And they use the same sort of domain structure as Wikipedia. eg. https://es.wikipedia.org and https://es.stackoverflow.com for the respective Spanish versions of Wikipedia and StackOverflow. Though they are not as well used nor as comprehensive as the English language version. For example, the English language version has ~430,000 pages of questions and the Spanish language version has ~13,000 pages of questions.

That said, I do not think StackOverflow makes the presence of the other languages versions as well known or accessible as Wikipedia does. For instance, on any Wikipedia page there is a widget that allows you to jump to an article on the same subject, but in a different language (if it exists). Maybe that is not as easy on StackOverflow as most questions will only get asked in one language and never duplicated to a different language. But that still does not excuse the lack of a prominent button or widget that makes it obvious that different versions of the website exist in different languages.

Q: Self-recursing-iterative functions in Python A:

I am not exactly sure why you start with add(), since Knuth's up-arrow notation, in its lowest level, starts with multiplication (compare Wikipedia article).

Anyway – a naive, straightforward implementation of the definition would be:

def i(a, b, arrows):
    if arrows == 1:
        return a ** b  # Break recursion at lowest level (one arrow)
    result = a
    for _ in range(b - 1):  # "- 1", because we init `result` with `a`
        result = i(a, result, arrows=arrows - 1)
    return result

Which we can sanity-check by some of the small results explicitly listed in the already mentioned Wikipedia article:

print(f"{i(2, 4, arrows=1)=:,}")
# i(2, 4, arrows=1)=16
print(f"{i(2, 4, arrows=2)=:,}")
# i(2, 4, arrows=2)=65,536
print(f"{i(3, 3, arrows=2)=:,}")
# i(3, 3, arrows=2)=7,625,597,484,987
print(f"{i(2, 3, arrows=3)=:,}")
# i(2, 3, arrows=3)=65,536

If you want to stay really true to the definition, you could replace a ** b by a for-loop as well, namely over multiplications. This, in turn, you could use to shorten and unify the code a bit more:

from operator import mul

def i(a, b, arrows):
    # Break recursion by explictly calling `mul()` for `arrows == 1`,
    # lower `i` by one arrow otherwise
    i_lower = mul if arrows == 1 else lambda a, b: i(a, b, arrows=arrows - 1)
    result = a
    for _ in range(b - 1):  # "- 1", because we init `result` with `a`
        result = i_lower(a, result)
    return result

A more functional implementation could be:

from functools import partial, reduce
from itertools import repeat
from operator import mul

def i(a, b, arrows):
    # Break recursion by explictly calling `mul()` for `arrows == 1`,
    # lower `i` by one arrow otherwise
    i_lower = mul if arrows == 1 else partial(i, arrows=arrows - 1)
    return reduce(lambda l, r: i_lower(r, l), repeat(a, times=b))

Here, I needed to reverse the parameters that reduce() passes to i_lower(), because reduce() reduces from left to right, while Knuth's up-arrow notation reduces from right to left. Arguably, this is a bit hard to read; in particular, as it may now seem that we calculate b↑…↑a rather than a↑…↑b, which is not the case (and which we can easily sanity-check, as above).

Q: Format for SilverLake ACHFileAdd field ACHFileConsmRefId A:

When using the ACHFileAdd a valid GUID for ACHFileConsmRefId is suggested but is not required. The ErrCat of Fault means you can override the error and use an identifier of your choosing. It would then be used to inquire/modify the ACH FIle that was sent in the ACHFIleAdd.

Q: Need help regarding open source contribution as a beginner A:

In terms of breaking things, I wouldn't worry too much. You're responsible for making a quality contribution, the project maintainers are responsible for checking if your contribution is ready to be merged into the project.

  1. Your testing should find issues that you introduce
  2. They might have automated tests that would find issues you introduce
  3. The reviewers should do manual testing that finds issues you introduce

You might also look for a wiki or a contributing.md file

Q: TO_DATE return an error in comparison but not as a column A:

Regarding the main issue, using TO_DATE on a column that's already a date is useless in this case so I removed it and it solved the problem, but still I suspect there's faulty data.

No, the fault is in the code not the data.

In Oracle, DATE data-type are stored as binary data consisting of 7 bytes representing century, year-of-century, month, day, hours, minutes and seconds. They ALWAYS have all of those components and they are NEVER stored in any particular human-readable format. If you have a DATE then it is almost certainly valid data (you have to try very hard to insert an invalid date into a DATE column and almost always it involves directly inserting binary data into the column which bypasses most of the usual checks).

The TO_DATE function takes a string as the first argument, if you pass something that is not a string then Oracle will implicitly try to convert your value to a string so your code. This implicit conversion is almost certainly causing the failure, not the underlying data.

Your code is effectively:

select *
from   MY_TABLE
where  ...
and    TO_DATE(
         TO_CHAR(
           CREATION_DATE,
           (SELECT value FROM NLS_SESSION_PARAMETERS WHERE parameter = 'NLS_DATE_FORMAT')
         ),
         'DD/MM/YYYY HH24:MI'
       ) > TO_DATE(
         TO_CHAR(
           current_date - INTERVAL '2' MONTH,
           (SELECT value FROM NLS_SESSION_PARAMETERS WHERE parameter = 'NLS_DATE_FORMAT')
         ),
         'DD/MM/YYYY HH24:MI'
       )

If the value of the NLS_DATE_FORMAT session parameter does not match the format mask DD/MM/YYYY HH24:MI then you are likely to get errors.

  • If the NLS_DATE_FORMAT is DD/MM/YYYY then you will get an error that the string is too short as it is missing the hours and minutes components.
  • If the NLS_DATE_FORMAT is YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI then you will get an error that the string invalid as it tries to parse the years and day and vice versa.
  • You are likely to get other values too.

Additionally, date_value - INTERVAL '2' MONTH will fail if today is the 31st day of the month and the the month two months before does not also have 31 days. Instead, you want to use ADD_MONTHS(date_value, -2) which will compensate for months having different numbers of days.

You appear to be trying to compare dates ignoring the seconds component of the date. To solve it:

  1. Use TRUNC:

    select *
from   MY_TABLE
where  ...
and    TRUNC(CREATION_DATE, 'MI')
         > TRUNC(ADD_MONTHS(current_date, -2), 'MI')

    Or, better, don't use TRUNC on the column as it allows Oracle to use an index on that column (if you do use a function on a column then Oracle would need a function-based index):

    select *
from   MY_TABLE
where  ...
and    CREATION_DATE
         >= TRUNC(ADD_MONTHS(current_date, -2), 'MI') + INTERVAL '1' MINUTE

  2. or, use TO_CHAR and specify the format modifiers in order of lowest to highest precision (i.e. YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI):

    select *
from   MY_TABLE
where  ...
and    TO_CHAR(CREATION_DATE, 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI')
       > TO_CHAR(ADD_MONTHS(current_date, -2), 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI')
